item.title: boxd Launches Self-Hosted Isolated MicroVMs for AI Agents and Developers
item.description:
boxd Launches Self-Hosted Isolated MicroVMs for AI Agents and Developers

A new self-hosted solution called boxd provides fast, isolated machines for AI agents and development teams to use as sandboxes, dev environments, or servers. The platform runs in your own Google Cloud project, AWS account, or on bare metal servers you already run, providing teams with a dedicated console, CLI, and API.

🔍 Overview

The platform allows teams to run fast microVMs that can be forked and snapshotted. Key features and capabilities include:

  • Flexible environments: MicroVMs can be used as agent sandboxes, development environments, or servers in the sizes you pick.
  • Network accessibility: Every VM is reachable over HTTPS and SSH, with support for custom domains and raw TCP or UDP ports.
  • AI Agent integration: The CLI comes with a built-in agent skill for Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode.
  • Broad authentication: Users can sign in with Google or GitHub, or via single sign-on through Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, or Keycloak.
  • Secured ingress: Supports private ingress on AWS, where no node has a public IP and users reach the cluster over a VPN.
  • Pricing: The platform is free for up to 16 worker vCPUs.

⚙️ How it works

The open-source installer sets up a complete boxd cluster from a single configuration file (cluster.toml) with one command. The only requirement on the local machine is Docker. The install script runs tested versions of Terraform, Ansible, gcloud, and the AWS CLI inside a Docker image.

Installation takes about an hour, with most of the time spent running the 20- to 40-minute apply process. Before any software is unpacked, the installer downloads and checks signed release binaries against release-keys. The cluster state, including TLS keys and provider secrets, is kept encrypted in a bucket you own (or in a local file next to cluster.toml for bare metal).

🧩 Cluster Architecture

A boxd cluster is composed of multiple node roles. While one node can have several roles, default examples put all roles except the worker on a single control node and add a single worker.

Node Role Description
Control nodes Run the cluster’s state over raft.
Workers Run the microVMs under KVM on boxd’s own host kernel.
Proxy Connects every VM to the internet at https://. and over SSH.
Console Serves the web console, the API, and a pre-configured CLI.
DNS node Answers for your registered DNS zone.
Metrics node Stores the graphs that are displayed for each VM in the console.

#AIagents #CloudComputing #DevOps #MicroVMs

item.title: Gitea Enables Self-Hosted Software Development Across All Go Platforms
item.description:
Gitea Enables Self-Hosted Software Development Across All Go Platforms

Gitea is a self-hosted all-in-one software development service designed to be the easiest, fastest, and most painless way to set up development infrastructure. It integrates Git hosting, code management, and team collaboration into a single platform.

🧩 How it works

Gitea is written in the Go programming language, which allows it to run across all platforms and architectures supported by Go. This includes:

  • Operating Systems: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, and Windows.
  • Architectures: x86, amd64, ARM, RISC-V 64, and PowerPC.

The system supports a comprehensive set of development tools, including:

  • Git hosting and code management
  • Code review and issue tracking
  • Project kanban and wiki functionality
  • Team collaboration
  • Package registry and CI/CD (which can reuse GitHub Actions)

⚙️ Key details

The project provides extensive documentation covering installation, administration, usage, and development. Key resources and commands include:

Resource Purpose
./gitea web Starts the server after building from source
./gitea help Displays all available commands
docs/build-source.md Instructions for building from source or creating distribution packages
docs/development.md Guides for setting up local environments, linting, and testing

For developers contributing to the project, the expected workflow is Fork → Patch → Push → Pull Request. Security vulnerabilities must be reported privately to security@gitea.io.

🚀 Availability

Users can access Gitea through several methods:

  • Online Demonstration: demo.gitea.com
  • Free Service: gitea.com offers a free service with a limited number of repositories.
  • Cloud Deployment: A free trial is available at cloud.gitea.com.
  • Container Deployment: The official image is available for Docker, Podman, or other container runtimes on your own server.
  • Community Support: Questions can be directed to the Discord server or the Discourse forum.

The ecosystem includes an official Go SDK, a CLI tool called gt, and an action runner for Gitea Actions. Third-party projects, SDKs, plugins, and themes are listed on the gitea/awesome-gitea repository.

item.title: GitHub Actions extension allows local workflow testing in VS Code
item.description:
GitHub Actions extension allows local workflow testing in VS Code

The GitHub Local Actions Visual Studio Code extension is now available, enabling developers to run and test GitHub Actions workflows locally without leaving their editor. This tool leverages the act tool to execute the set of actions defined in .github/workflows/ files by using Docker to pull or build necessary images and run containers for each action.

💡 Why it matters

  • Fast Feedback: Instead of committing and pushing changes to test modifications to .github/workflows/ files, developers can use act to run actions locally.
  • Local Task Runner: The extension allows GitHub Actions to replace Makefile functionality, addressing the need to avoid repeating tasks.
  • Environment Parity: The environment variables and filesystem are configured to match what GitHub provides for hosted runners.

🧩 How it works

When act is executed, it reads GitHub Actions from the .github/workflows/ directory and determines the execution path based on defined dependencies. The process involves:

  • Using the Docker API to pull or build necessary images as defined in workflow files.
  • Running containers for each action based on the prepared images.
  • Matching environment variables and filesystem configurations to GitHub’s standards.

⚙️ Key details

  • Documentation: The act user guide is available at nektosact.com.
  • Community Support: Users can ask for help in the project’s discussions section on GitHub.
  • Contributing: Developers can contribute by following the guidelines found in the CONTRIBUTING.md file.
  • Development Requirements: Building and installing the tool requires Go (version 1.26.0) and Docker. Unit tests are run via make test, while fast tests without Docker use make test-fast.

item.title: Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance
item.description:
Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance

Kong or Kong Gateway is a cloud-native, platform-agnostic, scalable API, LLM, and MCP Gateway distinguished for its high performance and extensibility via plugins. It provides advanced AI traffic capabilities with multi-LLM support, semantic security, MCP traffic security and analytics, and more.

🔍 Overview

Kong serves as the central layer for orchestrating microservices or conventional API traffic - and agentic LLM and MCP as well - with ease. By providing functionality for proxying, routing, load balancing, health checking, and authentication, it manages traffic across various architectures.

⚙️ Key details

  • Universal LLM API: Routes traffic across multiple providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, GCP Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure AI, Databricks, Mistral, and Huggingface.
  • MCP Capabilities: Includes MCP traffic governance, security, observability, and autogeneration from any RESTful API.
  • AI Features: Offers over 60 features such as AI observability, semantic security, caching, and semantic routing.
  • Security and Routing: Supports authentication and authorization via JWT, basic auth, OAuth, and ACLs.
  • Traffic Management: Handles proxying, SSL/TLS termination, and connectivity support for L4 or L7 traffic.
  • Plugins: Includes 60+ plugins for traffic controls, rate limiting, request/response transformations, logging, and monitoring.
Feature Description
Advanced Routing Load balancing and health checking configurable via RESTful admin API or declarative configuration
Deployment Models Supports Declarative Databaseless Deployment and Hybrid Deployment with control plane/data plane separation
Kubernetes Support Runs natively on Kubernetes thanks to its official Kubernetes Ingress Controller
Plugin Hub Showcases Kong Inc. and community-developed plugins like AWS Lambda, Correlation ID, and Response Transformer

🚀 Availability

Kong is available in various distributions depending on the deployment environment. Users can run it in the cloud, on bare metal, or using containers.

  • Cloud: Sign up for a free trial of Kong Konnect to get started with a cloud-hosted solution.
  • Docker: The docker-compose distribution is suggested for easy setup. A docker installation procedure is also available for running the Kong Gateway in DB-less mode.
  • Installation: To start with the Docker distribution, clone the Docker repository and navigate to the compose folder. Use the command $ KONG_DATABASE=postgres docker-compose --profile database up to start the Gateway stack.

Once started, the Gateway is available on localhost with the following ports:

  • 8000: Send traffic to your service via Kong.
  • 8001: Configure Kong using Admin API or via decK.
  • 8002: Access Kong’s management Web UI (Kong Manager).

A new Kubernetes mutating webhook has been developed to automate the injection of sidecar containers into pod specifications. This tool simplifies the management of sidecars within a Kubernetes cluster.

  • Namespace Watching: By default, the webhook monitors all namespaces except kube-system and kube-public.

item.title: Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes
item.description:
Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes

The Weaviate Helm chart has released version 17.1.0, introducing significant updates to cluster bootstrapping in Weaviate v1.25 and removing default resource constraints to improve module performance.

🔍 Overview

Weaviate can be deployed to a Kubernetes cluster using the provided Helm chart, provided that Helm is installed. Version 17.1.0 of the chart addresses specific infrastructure changes required by newer Weaviate releases and resolves performance restrictions in default configurations.

⚙️ Key Details: Cluster Bootstrapping

Weaviate v1.25 introduced a significant change in how the cluster bootstraps, driven by the adoption of a Raft-based consensus model.

  • The podManagementPolicy was changed from OrderedReady to Parallel.
  • This change is required for the Raft cluster to bootstrap properly, as all pods must start simultaneously.
  • Once the Raft cluster is established, rolling updates are possible.
  • This change takes effect when migrating from versions prior to v1.25 or when bootstrapping a new v1.25 cluster.

⚠️ Migration Steps

When upgrading from a version older than v1.25 to v1.25 or above, the following one-time operation is required:

  1. Delete Weaviate’s Statefulset.
  2. Update the Statefulset settings to reflect the new policy.

This process will not remove your data but is necessary to make the update of Statefulset settings possible.

📉 Key Details: Resource Limits

In Weaviate-Helm version 17.1.0, the default resource limits and requests defined in the values.yml file have been removed.

  • Reason: Previous default values restricted the performance of some modules, making them almost unusable unless resources.requests and resources.limits were overridden.
  • Impact: Modules deployed with default values prior to version 17.1.0 will have their resource values removed upon upgrading to 17.1.0 or above, resulting in no constraints on memory or CPU usage.
  • Recommendation: To prevent modules from consuming all system resources, users are strongly recommended to override modules.$MODULE.resources.requests and modules.$MODULE.resources.limits with values that suit their specific system.

🛠 Release Process

To release a new version of the chart, the following steps are taken:

  • Bump the chart version in ./weaviate/Chart.yaml.
  • Create a commit and an annotated tag matching the version number (prefixed with v, e.g., v1.4.3).
  • Push the commit and tag to the repository.
  • A GitHub Action creates a drafted release with the packaged chart attached.
  • The draft is edited to include release notes and published.

item.title: New Structural-Validation Evaluation Harness for Java LLM Codegen Service
item.description:
New Structural-Validation Evaluation Harness for Java LLM Codegen Service

📚 Introduction

A new structural-validation evaluation harness has been introduced for a Java LLM codegen service, designed to make A/B changes measurable and provide deterministic metrics instead of relying on demo screenshots or subjective assessments.

🔍 Overview

The harness implements a two-tier evaluation approach:

  • Runs benchmark prompts against a local Java service
  • Captures generated code through SSE
  • Evaluates outputs with deterministic structural checks
  • Optional browser execution smoke checks
  • Records raw JSON plus Markdown reports
  • Attributes tokens with per-run Prometheus counter windows

The most important finding was not a token percentage but a discovered issue: an earlier token result was polluted by Redis MessageWindowChatMemory carryover on a shared appId.

🧩 How it Works

The evaluation system operates through several components:

  • Kubernetes manifests serve Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B through vLLM
  • Infrastructure spans infra/azure (AKS/ACR/node pools) and infra/workloads (Terraform-managed inference/evaluation workloads)
  • A read-only authenticated GraphQL API queries both legacy Java reports and new serving runs
  • A bounded-concurrency benchmark records TTFT, p50/p95 latency, request/token throughput and structural quality

⚙️ Key Details

The structural pass@k evaluation found:

Metric Result
Structural pass@3 90.0% -> 90.0%
Total tokens 323,192 -> 317,785 (-1.7%)
CodeGen-stage input reduction ~18%

The harness identified a Java product bug: loadChatHistoryToMemory(...) returned before chatMemory.clear() when MySQL history was empty, causing prompt-composition diagnostics to reveal most of the CodeGen prompt was carried-over history.

Additional capabilities include:

  • Optional direct OpenAI-compatible inference reusing HTML evaluators and raw result format
  • Execution smoke checker validates known browser fixtures
  • One-shot repair path validates on a deterministic fixture
  • Replay / fixture mode validates offline report and evaluator paths
  • Failure taxonomy classifies report failures by layer

🚀 Availability

Documentation is available in three parts:

  • Part 1 deployment and recording guide
  • Part 2 Azure guide
  • Part 3 query and recording guide

Additional references:

  • RESULTS.md for full claim audit
  • Redis chat-memory carryover postmortem for incident write-up
  • LoRA/QLoRA SFT and held-out evaluation for deterministic data preparation and training provenance

💡 Why It Matters

The structural-validation pass@k differs from HumanEval-style evaluation:

  • It measures deterministic structural correctness, not functional correctness
  • Execution smoke validation serves as a thin second layer for narrow browser/build sanity, not full functional testing
  • The two layers are reported separately to avoid collapsing into one ambiguous pass number

Implementation tests are offline, and actual GPU deployment and performance measurements are pending. The sample data serves as a pipeline smoke fixture, with GPU training and quality gains remaining unverified.

item.title: MATE and OpenAgent Add Production Orchestration and Visual Workflows
item.description:
MATE and OpenAgent Add Production Orchestration and Visual Workflows

Two new AI development platforms, MATE and OpenAgent, have emerged to address the complexity of moving from single-agent experiments to production-grade multi-agent systems. MATE serves as a control layer that adds operational capabilities like versioning and cost tracking without requiring changes to the underlying agent code. Simultaneously, OpenAgent provides a full-stack platform for building, orchestrating, and publishing AI applications with deep reasoning loops and visual workflow authoring.

🧩 MATE: The Production Control Layer

MATE is a self-hosted, multi-agent orchestration engine built on Google ADK or LangGraph. It is designed to manage agent hierarchies, tool attachments, and prompt editing on a visual canvas. The platform supports any of 50+ LLM providers and includes persistent memory, web dashboard capabilities, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).

Key Operational Features

  • Configuration Management: Prompts, models, and user access permissions can be changed from a dashboard without code changes or redeployments.
  • Versioning and Rollback: Every configuration change is live, versioned, and allows for one-click rollback to any previous state.
  • Cost Tracking: Model calls are priced in US dollars as they are logged, supporting budgets that can warn or block based on spend.
  • Monitoring and Alerts: The system includes audit logs, guardrails, and alerts sent to Slack, Discord, email, or webhooks.
  • Trace Replay: A feature that plays back execution on a canvas, showing the order agents ran, hand-offs to sub-agents, models used, duration, and fallback usage.
  • Integration Options: Offers an embeddable chat widget, an OpenAI-compatible API, A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol support, and serves every agent as an MCP server.

Deployment and Case Studies

MATE can be deployed via Docker using the command docker run -d -p 8000:8000 -e AUTH_PASSWORD=change-me -e GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-key ghcr.io/antiv/mate:latest. The platform has been adopted by MVP-Soft, LLC, a US software consultancy, and Goal Navigator, which runs on MATE in production. Created by Ivan Antonijević, MATE also features a murder mystery demo and a browser-based wizard for provisioning agents, with an interface available in Serbian.

🖼️ OpenAgent: Visual Workflows and Deep Reasoning

OpenAgent is an end-to-end AI agent platform described as a full-stack solution for teams building AI applications. It combines a Flask backend with LangChain/LangGraph and a Vue 3 frontend workspace. The repository includes Celery workers, visual workflow authoring, dataset management, and public app publishing via OpenAPI.

Platform Capabilities

  • Visual Workflow Design: Users can design workflows using nodes for LLMs, tool calls, dataset retrieval, code execution, HTTP requests, branching, text processing, and structured parameter extraction.
  • Deep Research Mode: Allows apps to decompose complex tasks and coordinate capabilities across multi-step execution for scenarios requiring deep reasoning.
  • Knowledge and Retrieval: Supports RAG, semantic retrieval, full-text retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using Weaviate and FAISS.
  • Publishing and Delivery: Exposes published apps over REST and SSE through POST /api/openapi/chat.
  • Model Integrations: Compatible with OpenAI, Atlas Cloud, DeepSeek, Grok, Google, Moonshot, Tongyi, Wenxin, Ollama, and Zhipu. Atlas Cloud integration is configured via ATLASCLOUD_API_KEY and ATLASCLOUD_API_BASE.

⚙️ Technical Architecture Comparison

Feature MATE OpenAgent
Core Framework Google ADK, LangGraph LangChain, LangGraph
Backend Self-hosted Docker Python, Flask, Celery, Redis, PostgreSQL
Frontend Web Dashboard Vue 3, Vite, TailwindCSS, Pinia, Vue Flow
Primary Focus Agent orchestration, cost control, RBAC Visual workflows, RAG, deep reasoning loops
Model Providers 50+ LLM providers OpenAI, DeepSeek, Grok, Google, and others
Deployment Docker container Docker Compose, Nginx

💡 Why It Matters

A single agent in a notebook is easy to manage, but a hierarchy of agents serving real users introduces significant operational complexity. Without a control layer, tweaking a prompt requires editing code, committing changes, and redeploying the entire system. Additionally, teams often cannot easily identify which specific agent or token type (prompt, response, or reasoning) is consuming their budget. MATE addresses this by acting as a control layer that adds production necessities like versioning and cost visibility without touching the agent code. OpenAgent extends this utility by providing a dedicated workspace for drafting, publishing, and analyzing AI apps, allowing natural-language requirements to be turned into new creation flows.

#AIAgents #Orchestration #LangGraph #LLM #DevOps

item.title: OpenHands Cloud Introduces Scheduled and Event-Driven Automation Execution Service
item.description:
OpenHands Cloud Introduces Scheduled and Event-Driven Automation Execution Service

A new automation execution service has been developed for OpenHands Cloud, providing support for both scheduled and event-driven automation workflows.

🔍 Overview

The Automation Service allows users to manage and execute agent workflows based on predefined schedules or external triggers. Key features include:

  • Scheduled Automations: Run OpenHands conversations on a cron schedule.
  • Event-Driven Automations: Trigger automations via webhooks, such as GitHub events.
  • API Key Management: Per-user API keys for secure automation access.
  • Run History: Track automation runs with status and results.

🧩 How it works

System responsibilities are divided across several components:

  • Automation Service: Owns automation definitions, cron scheduling, webhooks, run history, dispatch, and sandbox lifecycle orchestration.
  • Agent Server and OpenHands/software-agent-sdk: Execute agent conversations and own agent/tool behavior, workspaces, events, and API endpoints.
  • OpenHands/typescript-client: Provides typed browser access to the Agent Server API.
  • OpenHands/OpenHands: Owns the Agent Canvas UI and frontend integration.

The codebase is structured into specific modules:

File Description
app.py FastAPI application entry point
router.py API routes for CRUD operations
scheduler.py Background scheduler for cron jobs
dispatcher.py Dispatches pending runs to OpenHands
models.py SQLAlchemy models
schemas.py Pydantic schemas for API

⚙️ Key details

The service is built using Python 3.12+ and uses uv for dependency management. For storage, it utilizes PostgreSQL, with testcontainers available for testing.

Database migration and creation rules include:

  • SQLite databases are migrated on startup.
  • PostgreSQL databases are not migrated on startup unless AUTOMATION_RUN_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP=true (or 1) is set. When set, each replica runs alembic upgrade head before serving requests, using an advisory lock so concurrent replicas take turns. A failed migration stops the replica from starting.
  • Setting AUTOMATION_CREATE_DATABASE_IF_MISSING=true (or 1) instructs migrations to connect to the postgres database and create the target database if missing. This requires the database user to have the CREATEDB privilege.

🚀 Deployment

For local development, dependencies can be installed using uv sync --group dev, and the application can be run with uv run uvicorn openhands.automation.app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload.

Container deployment can be built and run using Docker:

  • docker build -t automation -f containers/Dockerfile .
  • docker run -p 8000:8000 automation

The service is deployed via the deploy repository at https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/deploy. Docker images are automatically built and pushed to ghcr.io/openhands/automation on every push to main and on tags.

#OpenHands #Automation #Python #FastAPI #DevOps

Source: OpenHands/automation

item.title: Circle K Deploys Automated Incident Triage Using Amazon Bedrock
item.description:
Circle K Deploys Automated Incident Triage Using Amazon Bedrock

This post was co‑written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K.

🔍 Overview

Circle K runs a cloud‑native infrastructure on AWS that powers point‑of‑sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric‑vehicle charging across more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores in 27 countries. The DevOps team monitors this environment with Grafana and receives alerts for container restarts, error‑rate spikes, latency issues, and failed deployments.

⚠️ Manual Triage Pain

When an alert fires, engineers typically spend 45–60 minutes repeating the same steps:

  • Review recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch.
  • Examine application traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
  • Check Amazon ECS task status.
  • Cross‑reference symptoms with internal runbooks stored in GitHub. The depth and speed of triage vary with each on‑call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service.

🤖 Solution: Agentic AI Triage with Amazon Bedrock

Circle K built an automated triage system that uses Amazon Bedrock, a fully managed service that makes foundation models available through a single API. The system employs an agentic AI architecture that investigates each incident autonomously and delivers a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing.

Key Bedrock Benefits

  • Single API access to multiple foundation models; models can be swapped without code changes.
  • Native integration with existing AWS IAM, VPC, and logging configurations.
  • Built‑in orchestration that lets agents call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents.
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases provide managed Retrieval‑Augmented Generation, handling ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards without a separate vector database.
  • Customer data is not shared with model providers nor used to train foundation models, satisfying Circle K’s security requirements.

🏗️ Architecture

The end‑to‑end flow starts with a Grafana alert and proceeds through AWS services as follows:

Component Role
Grafana alert Publishes a notification to Amazon SNS
Amazon SNS Forwards the notification to an Amazon SQS queue
Amazon SQS Holds the alert payload for processing
AWS Lambda Polls the queue, extracts the payload, and invokes an Amazon Bedrock Flow
Amazon Bedrock Flow Orchestrates two parallel agents that perform log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups
Slack Receives the structured incident summary

📊 Impact

Since deployment, Circle K’s mean triage time has dropped to under 15 minutes—a 67–75 percent reduction according to internal incident‑response metrics. On‑call engineers now receive actionable context instead of raw alerts, allowing immediate remediation.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock model availability varies by AWS Region; refer to the “Supported models by AWS Region” documentation for details.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Consistent, fast triage reduces mean time to resolution.
  • Reduces manual effort and reliance on individual engineer expertise.
  • Meets strict security requirements by keeping sensitive operational data within the customer’s AWS account.
  • Eliminates the overhead of self‑hosting foundation models, prompting, versioning, and tool orchestration.

#AI #IncidentTriage #AmazonBedrock #DevOps

item.title: Hodor: An Agentic LLM‑Powered Code Reviewer for Git Repositories

Hodor: An Agentic LLM‑Powered Code Reviewer for Git Repositories

A new AI tool called Hodor provides an agentic code reviewer that can be run on GitHub pull requests, GitLab merge requests, Gitea/Forgejo pull requests, and local diffs.

🔍 Overview

  • Reviews code changes by invoking an LLM agent with confined inspection tools (git_diff, read, grep, find, ls).
  • Returns structured findings as inline comments and a summary note, or prints them locally.
  • Supports a default review protocol that remains unchanged unless explicitly overridden.

🧩 How it works

  1. Hodor checks out the change and automatically resolves to the git repository root, even when invoked from a subdirectory.
  2. It supplies the LLM with the limited toolset listed above and asks for a structured review.
  3. Findings are posted as inline comments and a summary, or output to the console.
  4. Optional instruction files can be added; they are additive, repeatable, and later files win conflicts, while --focus instructions win over file‑based instructions.
  5. The --profile security flag prefixes the bundled security‑review instructions before any explicit instruction files, narrowing reporting to security vulnerabilities without replacing the baseline protocol.

⚙️ Key details

  • Included changes: uncommitted (staged + unstaged) changes, not only committed code.
  • Repository handling: skips PR metadata fetching and workspace cloning.
  • Default model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.
  • Reasoning effort: Adaptive.
  • Optional flags:
    • --ultrathink – Off
    • --full – Off
    • --post – disabled (no remote posting)
    • --target-branch – None
  • Supported LLM providers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, OpenRouter; other providers are best‑effort.

--model anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 Base LLM used for the review
--reasoning-effort Adaptive Level of reasoning effort applied
--ultrathink Off Extended reasoning mode (disabled)
--full Off Full‑snapshot review mode (disabled)
--post Disabled Remote posting of comments (disabled)
--target-branch None Branch to compare against (none by default)

🚀 Availability

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables consistent, automated code reviews across multiple Git platforms without requiring repository cloning.
  • Allows security‑focused reviews via --profile security or --focus "Report only security findings." while preserving baseline defect checks.
  • Supports a range of LLM back‑ends, making it adaptable to existing infrastructure.

item.title: Encore expands platform for building production systems with real infrastructure
item.description:
Encore expands platform for building production systems with real infrastructure

Encore released an update that adds new capabilities for building, testing, and deploying production‑grade systems using real infrastructure throughout the development lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

Encore is the infrastructure platform for the intelligence era, where engineers and AI agents build production systems without waiting on infrastructure.

🧩 How It Works

  • Run and validate with real infrastructure locally and in preview environments, then deploy to your own AWS or GCP account.
  • Declare the resources your app needs (databases, Pub/Sub, object storage, caches, cron jobs, secrets) directly in your code, and encore run starts the whole system locally with real Postgres, real Pub/Sub semantics, and distributed tracing.
  • Each declaration becomes a node in Encore’s application graph.
  • Encore runs the migrations and stands up local equivalents on encore run, and provisions the cloud equivalents on deploy.
  • When you push a change that adds or modifies a resource, Encore diffs the application graph against the environment, provisions whatever is missing in your AWS or GCP account, and rolls out the new code against it.
  • Encore separates application semantics from environment-specific configuration.
  • In code, you define what resources your app needs, not how each environment should configure them.
  • That keeps services portable across clouds, regions, accounts, scale profiles, and local development.
  • Encore provisions every resource with sane production defaults, then helps you manage configuration separately from your application code.

⚙️ Key Features

  • Encore platform dashboard: easy to use knobs for all common settings like process allocation, instance sizes, replicas, etc.
  • Your AWS or GCP console: tweak anything directly in your cloud provider console.
  • Encore picks up the changes on the next deploy.
  • IaC: manage config for Encore‑provisioned resources alongside the rest of your infrastructure via the Terraform provider.
  • The same infrastructure model runs locally, in per‑PR preview environments, and in production.
  • Local: encore run starts the whole system locally: real Postgres, real Pub/Sub semantics, type‑safe service‑to‑service calls, plus a local dashboard with distributed tracing.
  • Infrastructure namespaces let multiple branches or agents work in parallel with isolated state.
  • Open a pull request and Encore sets up an ephemeral environment and (optionally) branches databases from a seed environment.
  • This Lets you do end‑to‑end validation against before merging to a shared staging environment.
  • Production: Push to deploy.

🚀 Availability

The update is available to users who already have Encore set up on AWS or GCP and can be accessed through the standard encore run and deployment commands.

💡 Why It Matters

By letting developers define what resources are needed rather than how each environment configures them, Encore makes services portable across clouds, regions, and accounts while keeping configuration separate from application code. The need for such caps has been highlighted by developers using coding agents that can quickly generate code which calls paid APIs, storage, or compute resources.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Hard limits required – “These need to be hard limits.”
  • Soft caps insufficient – “Soft caps, “after $X/month, send me a warning email”, will not cut it.”
  • Desired default behavior – “I think hard budget caps need to be the default.”
  • Opt‑in for risk‑takers – “If someone wants to live dangerously they should be able to do that, but it needs to be on an opt‑in basis.”
  • Business preference – “I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill.”

AWS Cloud Development Kit Enables Infrastructure Definition Using Modern Programming Languages

The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) is an open-source software development framework designed to define cloud infrastructure in code and provision it through AWS CloudFormation. It offers high-level object-oriented abstractions to define AWS resources imperatively using several modern programming languages.

🔍 Overview

The CDK allows developers to encapsulate AWS best practices within infrastructure definitions using a library of infrastructure constructs. This approach aims to reduce the complexity and glue-logic typically required when integrating various AWS services. By using the framework, developers can share infrastructure definitions without managing boilerplate logic.

🧩 How it works

Developers use the CDK framework in one of the supported programming languages to build components through a specific hierarchy:

  • Constructs: Reusable cloud components that encapsulate the details of how to use AWS.
  • Stacks: Compositions of constructs grouped together.
  • CDK App: The final application formed by one or more stacks.

Developers interact with their applications using the AWS CDK CLI. The CLI allows for the synthesis of artifacts such as AWS CloudFormation Templates, the deployment of stacks to development AWS accounts, and the ability to “diff” against a deployed stack to understand the impact of code changes.

⚙️ Key details

The AWS Construct Library includes modules for each AWS service. These modules are assigned stability designations that determine how they are updated:

Stability Designation Versioning Policy
Experimental Modules currently being built; may have breaking API changes in any release.
Stable Adheres to semantic versioning; breaking changes can only occur in major releases.

🚀 Availability

The AWS CDK is available for several programming languages with specific environment requirements:

Language Requirements
JavaScript / TypeScript Node.js >= 20.x
Python Python >= 3.8
Java Java >= 8 and Maven >= 3.5.4

AWS Introduces Serverless Automation for Git Metrics and AI-DLC Observability

AWS has introduced a serverless approach to automate the collection of Git metrics from GitHub and GitLab. This solution integrates with Amazon Quick Sight to provide live analytics and align with the observability pillar of the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework.

💡 Why it matters

Git activity provides continuous observability into development analytics, but extracting these metrics at scale has traditionally required dedicated infrastructure and hand-rolled extract, transform, and load (ETL) jobs. According to the AI-DLC framework, organizations using AI coding tools need numbers to quantify if AI is increasing speed, merely padding commit counts, or introducing unexpected quality issues.

🧩 How it works

The solution implements an automated, event-driven pipeline using six core AWS services:

Service Function
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Starts the workflow at a configured interval using rate() or cron() expressions.
AWS Step Functions Orchestrates the collection workflow and decides between full and incremental loads.
AWS Lambda Handles separate chunks of repository processing.
AWS Secrets Manager Securely stores Git tokens.
Amazon S3 Persists results for visualization.
Amazon Quick Sight Provides interactive dashboards for graphical visualization.

⚙️ Key details

The architecture includes several specialized mechanisms for efficient data collection:

  • Intelligent change detection: A detector function monitors GitLab activity feeds and the GitHub events API to identify changes in commits, pull requests, issues, or repository creation and deletion.
  • Full and incremental loads: The system performs a full load of all repository metadata on the first execution and triggers a full refresh every 24 hours. Incremental loads collect only data changed since the last run to reduce execution time and API calls.
  • Adaptive chunking: For organizations with more than 20 repositories, the workload is automatically partitioned into parallel chunks processed concurrently via Step Functions Map states.
  • Infrastructure: The serverless design abstracts infrastructure management to remain low-cost at scale.

item.description:
AWS Expands Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AI-DLC Reference Implementations

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a service for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale with any framework or model, now powers two new reference implementations that demonstrate AI-DLC construction phase patterns. AI-DLC positions AI as a central collaborator across the software development lifecycle, handling routine execution while humans retain oversight of critical decisions.

🔍 Overview

The two reference implementations cover:

  • Automated generation of Mermaid entity relationship diagrams from SQL schemas
  • Automated code security analysis through a multi-agent architecture

Both implementations link to complete deployment instructions in their respective GitHub repositories.

🧩 How It Works

Mermaid ER Diagram Generator

This AWS Samples project auto-generates Mermaid ER diagrams from SQL schema files using an agentic AI workflow on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Architecture components:

Component Function
S3 event trigger SQL files uploaded to Amazon S3 trigger an AWS Lambda function that initiates the analysis workflow
Amazon Cognito Provides OAuth2 machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Stores client credentials
AgentCore runtime Containerized agent built with the Strands framework
AgentCore memory Persistent session context with 90-day expiry, supports semantic search across previous analyses
Amazon S3 Output storage for generated .mmd files under dedicated prefix with metadata tracking

Workflow:

  • SQL file is uploaded to Amazon S3 (manually or through CI/CD pipeline)
  • Lambda trigger reads file content and authenticates through Cognito OAuth
  • Trigger invokes AgentCore runtime agent with SQL content as payload
  • Agent analyzes schema and identifies tables, columns, constraints, and foreign key relationships
  • Agent generates complete Mermaid erDiagram
  • Diagram is saved to Amazon S3 and analysis session is stored in AgentCore memory

Key design decisions:

  • Chunked processing: Large SQL files split into manageable segments, analyzed independently, then consolidated
  • Structured prompting: Systematic analysis prompt extracts tables, columns, data types, primary keys, and foreign key relationships before generating diagram syntax
  • OpenTelemetry tracing: Every step instrumented with spans and attributes for observability into processing duration, chunk counts, and error attribution

The agent uses Claude Sonnet 4 through Amazon Bedrock to parse SQL DDL statements. It reads only schema metadata (tables, constraints, and foreign keys), never row data.

Automated Code Security Analysis

The second implementation provides automated code security analysis through a multi-agent architecture that uses:

  • AgentCore Gateway
  • AgentCore memory
  • External tool integrations

This system analyzes code pushed through CI/CD pipelines, producing security assessments, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) checks, and policy compliance reports that inform human decision-making.

⚙️ Key Details

Both systems share a common architectural foundation built on AgentCore, demonstrating how teams can compose AI-driven workflows from modular, manageable components.

The AI-DLC construction phase positions AI to:

  • Propose architecture
  • Generate implementation plans
  • Produce code
  • Create deployment artifacts

Team members provide clarification on technical decisions in real time.

🚀 Availability

The complete implementation for the Mermaid ER diagram generator is available in its GitHub repository. The automated code security analysis implementation is also available with complete deployment instructions.

💡 Why It Matters

Database teams managing evolving SQL schemas need current entity relationship documentation. Manual creation of ER diagrams is time-intensive and documentation frequently drifts from the actual schema. When schema changes land through pull requests, teams need updated diagrams without adding manual documentation steps to the development workflow.

For security, continuous code quality enforcement through multi-agent systems ensures that assessments, CVE checks, and policy compliance reports inform human decision-making rather than replacing it.

Paca: Open-Source AI-Native Project Management for Scrum Teams

A new self-hosted project management platform, Paca, introduces AI agents as equal collaborators within Scrum teams, offering a free and fully customizable alternative to tools like Jira and Trello.

🔍 Overview

Paca integrates AI agents directly into Scrum workflows, enabling them to work alongside humans on shared boards, sprints, and goals. Key features include:

  • AI agents assigned to sprints and visible on Scrumban boards
  • Real-time task updates from backlogs
  • AI contributions to BDD specs (Gherkin) and system design documents
  • Lightweight, open-source core (Apache 2.0 license)

🧩 How it works

Paca embeds AI agents into team workflows through configurable plugins and project-level settings. Agents actively:

  • Pick up tasks and update statuses dynamically
  • Collaborate on technical documentation
  • Adapt to emerging complexity via sensing/response mechanisms

Plugin System

Plugin Type Description Examples
Backend (WASM) Extends routes, logic, data models Custom sprint rules, data fields
Frontend (Modules) Adds UI pages, board views, widgets Specialized dashboards, workflows

⚙️ Key details

  • Fully customizable: Workflows, boards, and agent behaviors configured via project files (no code)
  • Sandbox security: Plugins run in capability-based permission environments
  • Architecture: Core platform remains minimal; all extensions are optional plugins
  • Sponsors: Supported by AWS, Neon, DigitalOcean, and Virtuals Protocol

🚀 Availability

Paca is immediately available as a free, self-hosted solution. Users can:

  • Install via Plugin Marketplace (Settings → Plugins → Marketplace)
  • Extend functionality through WASM/frontend plugins
  • Access 100% open-source code under Apache 2.0

💡 Why it matters

Paca pioneers human-AI collaboration as equal teammates in Scrum, eliminating AI as a peripheral tool. Its open-source flexibility and plugin ecosystem allow teams to tailor processes without vendor lock-in.

item.title: DevOps Agent Introduces Custom Memory Stores for Operational Knowledge
item.description:
DevOps Agent Introduces Custom Memory Stores for Operational Knowledge

The August 27, 2026, update to the DevOps Agent enables users to create custom memory stores, providing a mechanism to retain operational knowledge across sessions. This update moves beyond previous limitations where memories were restricted to automatically learned monitors or user-input directives.

🧩 How it works

Memory stores act as a repository for reusable conclusions, such as infrastructure quirks, component relationships, and root causes of recurring incidents.

  • Organization: Users can create a hierarchy by using / separators in memory names, creating a folder-like structure.
  • Progressive Disclosure: The agent utilizes the name and description of a store to determine relevance, reading only the necessary files rather than the entire content.
  • Custom Agents: Memory stores can be attached to custom agents, which are then restricted to reading from and writing to only those assigned stores.

⚙️ Key details

Store Type Access Level Description
Managed Read-only Stores learned skills like topology, dependencies, and tool usage patterns.
Custom Read/Write User-defined stores for specific teams, services, or issues.

💡 Why it matters

This update allows teams to carry over knowledge that would otherwise be lost between investigation sessions. By recording communication preferences, instructions, and infrastructure patterns, the agent can skip duplicate diagnostic steps and behave more consistently according to established team knowledge.

#DevOps #AIAgents #CloudOperations #Automation

🚀 AI Revolution in QA: 10 Testing Tools That Will Transform Your Software Development in 2025

Summary: Discover how AI is revolutionizing software testing with 10 cutting-edge tools set to dominate in 2025. From visual testing and API automation to codeless solutions that empower every team member, these intelligent platforms will help you deliver higher quality software faster while dramatically reducing manual testing efforts.

🔮 The AI Testing Transformation Has Arrived

The software development landscape is undergoing a seismic shift. As applications grow increasingly complex and release cycles shrink, traditional testing approaches are struggling to keep pace. The solution? Artificial intelligence has entered the testing arena, and it’s changing everything.

AI-powered testing isn’t just an incremental improvement—it’s a complete paradigm shift. These intelligent systems learn from your data, adapt to changes automatically, and help your team focus on creativity rather than repetitive tasks. The results are dramatic: faster releases, more thorough testing coverage, and significantly fewer production bugs.

Let’s explore the top 10 AI testing tools that will define excellence in 2025, and why you should be integrating them into your workflow right now.

🧠 Why AI Testing Is No Longer Optional

Before diving into the tools, let’s understand why AI testing has become essential:

  • 🔄 Self-healing tests: AI-powered tests can adapt to UI changes, drastically reducing maintenance overhead
  • 🔍 Enhanced bug detection: AI identifies patterns and anomalies humans might miss
  • ⚡ Accelerated testing cycles: Automation of repetitive tasks speeds up the entire pipeline
  • 📊 Improved coverage: AI can generate test scenarios beyond what human testers might conceive

Traditional testing often leaves gaps and relies heavily on manual maintenance. AI testing tools fill those gaps while continuously improving themselves through machine learning.

🛠️ 10 AI Testing Tools Reshaping QA in 2025

1. Apidog: The API Testing Revolution

𝗔𝗽𝗶𝗱𝗼𝗴 is transforming API testing with its comprehensive AI-powered platform. What makes it exceptional is how it handles your entire API lifecycle—from design and documentation to testing and monitoring—all in one place.

Key capabilities:

  • AI-generated test scenarios based on your API specifications
  • Automated documentation that stays in sync with your API changes
  • Smart test maintenance that adapts to API evolution

Apidog’s intelligent approach means you’ll spend less time writing repetitive tests and more time ensuring your APIs deliver business value.

2. Applitools Eyes: Visual AI That Sees Like a Human

Visual regression testing has traditionally been error-prone and tedious. 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝗘𝘆𝗲𝘀 changes this with its groundbreaking visual AI technology that understands layouts and components—not just pixels.

This tool can detect even the subtlest UI issues across browsers, devices, and screen sizes with remarkable accuracy. Its AI algorithms understand the difference between meaningful changes and insignificant variations, dramatically reducing false positives.

3. Testim: Self-Healing Test Automation

𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺’s adaptive AI engine creates stable, resilient tests that evolve alongside your application. Its most impressive feature is the self-healing capability—tests automatically adjust to UI changes without requiring constant maintenance.

Each test execution makes the system smarter, continuously improving reliability and reducing flakiness over time.

4. Functionize: Testing in Plain English

Perhaps the most accessible tool on our list, 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗲 allows team members to create tests using natural language. Its NLP engine transforms English descriptions into sophisticated test scenarios, democratizing testing across your organization.

This means product managers, business analysts, and other non-technical stakeholders can contribute to test creation without writing code.

5. TestCraft: Visual Test Creation with AI Resilience

𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗖𝗿𝗮𝗳𝘁’s visual approach combines drag-and-drop simplicity with powerful AI that maintains test stability. Its canvas-based interface lets you build complex test scenarios visually while its AI engine handles the technical complexity behind the scenes.

The platform’s real-time monitoring capabilities provide immediate feedback, helping you identify issues as they emerge rather than after they’ve affected users.

6. Mabl: Intelligent End-to-End Testing

𝗠𝗮𝗯𝗹 excels at end-to-end testing with its comprehensive AI-driven insights. It automatically detects visual changes, JavaScript errors, and performance issues all while integrating seamlessly with popular CI/CD tools.

Its intelligent test execution prioritizes the most critical tests based on recent code changes, helping teams get faster feedback on high-risk areas.

7. Perfecto: AI-Powered Testing at Scale

Cloud-based 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼 tackles one of the biggest challenges in modern development—testing across countless device and browser combinations. Its AI capabilities help identify the optimal testing matrix and detect patterns in test failures.

The platform’s intelligent reporting quickly pinpoints the root cause of issues, distinguishing between device-specific bugs and broader application problems.

8. Sauce Labs: Real-World Testing Intelligence

𝗦𝗮𝘂𝗰𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗯𝘀 combines massive test infrastructure with AI-driven analytics to give you confidence your application works everywhere. Its machine learning algorithms analyze test results to identify patterns and suggest improvements.

The platform’s real-time insights help teams understand not just that tests failed, but why they failed and how to fix them most efficiently.

9. Katalon Studio: All-in-One AI Testing

𝗞𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 brings AI capabilities to web, mobile, and API testing in a unified platform. Its unique strength is combining script-based and codeless approaches, making it accessible to testers of all experience levels.

The AI-assisted test creation suggests test steps and helps identify optimal selectors, dramatically accelerating test development.

10. BrowserStack: AI Testing on Real Devices

𝗕𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘀𝗲𝗿𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸’s vast real device cloud paired with AI-powered insights ensures your applications work flawlessly across the digital landscape. Its intelligent test orchestration optimizes execution time and provides actionable recommendations.

The platform’s AI capabilities help predict which device/browser combinations are most likely to experience issues based on your specific application.

🚀 Embracing the AI Testing Future

As we look toward 2025, it’s clear that AI-powered testing tools will become standard components of successful development practices. These intelligent systems don’t just automate existing processes—they fundamentally transform how we approach quality assurance.

The organizations that thrive will be those that embrace these tools early, integrating them into their workflows and upskilling their teams. The most significant advantage isn’t just speed or cost reduction—it’s the ability to deliver dramatically better software experiences to users.

Among these transformative tools, Apidog stands out for teams looking to modernize their API testing approach with a comprehensive, AI-driven solution that spans the entire API lifecycle.

item.description:
🔍 EKS Dashboard: The Command Center Your Multi-Region Kubernetes Fleet Desperately Needs

📊 Summary

AWS unleashes EKS Dashboard, a game-changing centralized visibility solution that eliminates multi-cluster management headaches. Now you can monitor all your Kubernetes clusters across AWS regions and accounts from a single pane of glass—no third-party tools required. This blog explores how this powerful native capability simplifies operations, enhances compliance tracking, and streamlines version management for enterprise-scale Kubernetes deployments.

🌐 The Multi-Cluster Management Challenge

Managing Kubernetes at scale has become increasingly complex for organizations running multiple clusters. As companies expand their containerized infrastructure footprint, they inevitably distribute clusters across different AWS regions and accounts for reasons including:

  • 🔄 Enhanced availability and failover capabilities
  • 🛡️ Business continuity requirements
  • 📍 Data sovereignty compliance
  • 🧪 Separation of development, testing, and production environments

But this distributed approach creates a visibility nightmare. Without centralized monitoring, cluster administrators face several challenges:

  • 🔎 Limited cross-region and cross-account visibility
  • ⏱️ Time-consuming manual inventory tracking
  • 📝 Difficulty in assessing version compliance
  • 🧩 Fragmented operational planning

Many organizations have resorted to third-party solutions to address these issues, but these come with their own complications:

  • Complex identity and access management setup
  • Additional licensing costs
  • Ongoing maintenance overhead

🚀 Enter EKS Dashboard: Visibility Simplified

AWS has now addressed this pain point with the introduction of the Amazon EKS Dashboard—a native AWS Console capability that provides that long-desired “single pane of glass” for all your Kubernetes clusters.

The EKS Dashboard delivers comprehensive insights into three critical resource types:

  • 🔵 EKS clusters
  • 🟢 Managed node groups
  • 🟣 EKS add-ons

What makes this particularly powerful is the aggregated visibility across your entire organization. At a glance, you can now see:

  • 🗺️ Cluster distribution by Region and account
  • 🔢 Version distribution across clusters
  • ⚠️ Support status indicators
  • 💰 Forecasted extended support costs for EKS control planes
  • 📊 Health metrics for all clusters

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘀𝗵𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮—𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲. With automatic filtering capabilities, you can quickly drill down to identify specific clusters needing attention, whether for upgrades, compliance issues, or other operational concerns.

⚙️ Simple Setup, Powerful Features

Setting up EKS Dashboard is refreshingly straightforward. Access is available through AWS Organizations’ management and delegated administrator accounts. The entire setup process consists of:

  1. 🔑 Enabling trusted access as a one-time setup in the Amazon EKS console’s organizations settings
  2. 🔄 Accessing the Dashboard settings page
  3. ✅ Confirming trusted access for the management account

Once configured, the dashboard offers multiple visualization options to help you understand your Kubernetes environment:

  • 📊 Graphical widgets for at-a-glance insights
  • 📋 Detailed tabular data for comprehensive analysis
  • 🗺️ Geographic map view showing cluster distribution across the globe
  • 🔍 Advanced filtering and search capabilities
  • 📤 Data export functionality for custom reporting needs

𝘓𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘶𝘭𝘢𝘳 𝘷𝘪𝘴𝘪𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺? The dashboard enables you to visualize your managed node groups by instance type distribution, launch templates, AMI versions, and numerous other parameters—perfect for identifying standardization opportunities or potential optimization points.

🌍 Beyond AWS: Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Support

Perhaps most impressively, EKS Dashboard isn’t limited to just AWS-native clusters. Organizations operating in hybrid or multi-cloud environments can also benefit from this tool, as it supports:

  • 🏢 On-premises Kubernetes clusters
  • ☁️ Kubernetes clusters on other cloud providers

While connected non-AWS clusters may provide somewhat limited data compared to native EKS clusters, this capability delivers truly unified visibility across diverse environments—addressing one of the most significant challenges in modern cloud-native operations.

🏁 Available Today with No Additional Cost

The EKS Dashboard is available now in the US East (N. Virginia) Region but can aggregate data from all commercial AWS Regions. And here’s the best part: there is 𝙣𝙤 𝙖𝙙𝙙𝙞𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙖𝙡 𝙘𝙝𝙖𝙧𝙜𝙚 for using this feature.

This release represents AWS’s ongoing commitment to reducing the operational burden of running Kubernetes at scale. By providing native tooling that eliminates the need for third-party solutions, AWS is enabling organizations to focus more on application development and less on infrastructure management.

🤔 The Bigger Picture

The introduction of EKS Dashboard reflects an important trend in cloud services: the recognition that visibility and operational simplicity are just as important as raw technical capabilities. As Kubernetes deployments continue to multiply across diverse environments, tools that consolidate and simplify management will become increasingly crucial.

For teams struggling with Kubernetes sprawl, this dashboard offers a welcome respite—a simple way to regain control and visibility without additional tooling complexity. Will this be the beginning of more sophisticated cross-account, cross-region management capabilities for AWS services? Only time will tell, but it’s certainly a step in the right direction.

How might your organization’s Kubernetes operations change with this level of consolidated visibility? And what other aspects of multi-cluster management would you like to see simplified next?

🔍 Digital Banking Revolution: How Nubank Leverages AWS and Honeycomb for Exceptional User Experience

Summary: Explore how Nubank, Latin America’s largest digital bank, transforms the financial landscape by implementing advanced observability with Honeycomb on AWS infrastructure. This analysis reveals their technical architecture, monitoring strategies, and the direct correlation between system performance and customer satisfaction in modern banking.

🚀 The New Face of Banking: Technology-First Approach

In the rapidly evolving landscape of financial technology, few success stories stand out like Nubank’s meteoric rise. As Latin America’s largest digital bank, Nubank has revolutionized banking in a region traditionally dominated by bureaucratic institutions with poor customer service reputations. But what powers this fintech giant’s ability to deliver exceptional customer experiences?

Behind Nubank’s sleek mobile interface lies a sophisticated technology stack built on AWS and enhanced with Honeycomb’s observability platform—a combination that delivers both reliability and insights critical for maintaining customer trust in financial services.

📸 See illustration below showing Nubank’s digital-first customer interface contrasted with traditional banking experiences

🏗️ Building a Resilient Banking Infrastructure on AWS

Nubank’s infrastructure leverages AWS’s ecosystem extensively, creating a robust foundation for serving millions of customers across Latin America. Their architecture demonstrates several key principles worth highlighting:

𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁

Nubank’s engineering team designed their systems to handle dramatic growth—from thousands to millions of customers—without requiring fundamental architectural changes. Their approach includes:

  • Auto-scaling microservices deployed across multiple AWS availability zones
  • Strategic use of Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) for container orchestration
  • Leveraging DynamoDB’s consistent performance characteristics for transaction processing

“𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘢𝘮𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘭𝘴𝘦,” is a philosophy that permeates Nubank’s technical decisions.

𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴

Financial services demand extraordinary reliability. Nubank achieves this through:

  • Multi-region deployments for disaster recovery
  • Circuit breakers and fallback mechanisms built into critical transaction paths
  • Blue/green deployment strategies minimizing customer impact during updates

🔥 A particularly interesting aspect is their implementation of asynchronous processing for non-critical operations, which maintains core service availability even during partial system failures.

🔮 Observability: Honeycomb as Nubank’s Crystal Ball

While AWS provides the foundation, Honeycomb delivers the visibility that transforms Nubank’s operations. Traditional monitoring tells you 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 something is wrong; Nubank’s observability approach with Honeycomb tells them 𝘄𝗵𝘆 it’s happening.

𝗕𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘀: 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵-𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮

Implementing Honeycomb allowed Nubank to move beyond simple metric collection to capturing and analyzing high-dimensional data across their services. Key benefits include:

  • Tracing individual customer transactions across dozens of microservices
  • Identifying performance bottlenecks affecting specific customer segments
  • Real-time debugging capabilities reducing mean time to resolution (MTTR)

📸 See illustration below showing Honeycomb’s visualization of a customer transaction flowing through Nubank’s systems

𝙐𝙨𝙚𝙧-𝘾𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙞𝙘 𝙊𝙗𝙨𝙚𝙧𝙫𝙖𝙗𝙞𝙡𝙞𝙩𝙮

Perhaps the most valuable aspect of Nubank’s observability implementation is its focus on customer experience metrics:

  • Correlation between system performance and customer satisfaction scores
  • Ability to trace poor experiences to specific code deployments
  • Proactive identification of issues before customers report them

“𝑊𝑒 𝑑𝑜𝑛’𝑡 𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡 𝑚𝑜𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑜𝑟 𝑠𝑒𝑟𝑣𝑖𝑐𝑒𝑠; 𝑤𝑒 𝑚𝑜𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑜𝑟 𝑐𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑜𝑚𝑒𝑟 𝑗𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑛𝑒𝑦𝑠,” exemplifies their philosophy.

🧠 Technical Decisions with Business Impact

One fascinating aspect of Nubank’s technical implementation is how deliberately they tie engineering decisions to business outcomes. Several examples stand out:

𝟭. 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲-𝗔𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴

Nubank’s team recognizes that perfect reliability comes at a cost. Their approach balances:

  • Identifying truly critical paths requiring 99.99%+ reliability
  • Accepting lower reliability targets for non-critical features
  • Creating degradation paths that maintain core functionality during incidents

𝟮. 𝗜𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗩𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆

The combination of AWS’s managed services and Honeycomb’s observability enables Nubank to innovate rapidly with confidence:

  • Feature flagging systems allowing controlled rollouts
  • Detailed before/after performance comparisons for new features
  • Quick validation of business hypotheses through real usage data

🔍 This capability to innovate rapidly without sacrificing stability represents a significant competitive advantage in the financial sector where traditional banks often move slowly.

𝟯. 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗢### 𝟯. 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻

Unlike traditional banks with enormous fixed infrastructure costs, Nubank takes advantage of AWS’s pay-for-what-you-use model while implementing sophisticated cost controls:

  • Detailed tagging strategies tracking expenditure across business domains
  • Right-sizing resources based on Honeycomb’s usage pattern insights
  • Automated scaling tied directly to business transaction volume

This approach has enabled Nubank to achieve a cost-per-customer that traditional banks can only dream of—creating flexibility to offer fee-free products that disrupt traditional banking models. 💰

🚨 Crisis Management: When Things Go Wrong

Even the best systems experience outages. What sets Nubank apart is their sophisticated incident response powered by observability:

𝗥𝗮𝗽𝗶𝗱 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲

When a payment processing slowdown occurred during a major shopping day, Nubank’s system:

  • Detected anomalies within seconds through Honeycomb’s real-time tracing
  • Automatically routed traffic away from degraded services
  • Provided engineers with precise diagnostic information to address root causes

“𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘪𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘵𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘢 15-𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 2-𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘢𝘨𝘦 𝘰𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘥𝘰𝘸𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘰𝘣𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺,” their CTO has noted.

𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀

Perhaps most impressive is how Nubank converts incidents into systemic improvements:

  • Automated post-incident analysis using Honeycomb data
  • Identification of patterns across seemingly unrelated incidents
  • Implementation of architectural improvements targeting underlying causes

🌟 The Future: AI-Enhanced Banking Infrastructure

Nubank isn’t resting on their success. Their technology roadmap reveals ambitious plans:

  • Machine learning models analyzing Honeycomb data to predict potential failures before they occur
  • AI-assisted routing optimizing transaction paths based on real-time system conditions
  • Personalized performance tuning based on individual customer usage patterns

“𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝙣𝙚𝙭𝙩 𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙥 𝙞𝙨 𝙣𝙤𝙩 𝙟𝙪𝙨𝙩 𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙥𝙤𝙣𝙙𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙩𝙤 𝙞𝙨𝙨𝙪𝙚𝙨 𝙦𝙪𝙞𝙘𝙠𝙡𝙮, 𝙗𝙪𝙩 𝙥𝙧𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙩𝙝𝙚𝙢 𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙡𝙮,” explains their Director of Engineering.

🎯 Key Takeaways: The Observability Advantage

Nubank’s success story offers valuable lessons for any organization building digital services:
